title: Foucault pendulum, Békéscsaba (real footage)

source.credit: Foucault pendulum in Békéscsaba, Hungary, filmed by Zátonyi Sándor (ifj.), FizFilm; real footage, cropped to the swing (0:20.5–1:02.5 of the original)

narration.transcript: This Foucault pendulum is 8.97 metres long.

caveats: motion is directly along the camera optical axis toward and away from camera
image size changes with distance so lateral scale is small
some motion blur on the bob at closest approach

reference.basis: whiteboard markers and floor tiles are not standard sizes, no A4 or metre stick visible

slow_motion.evidence: no caption or narration indicates slow motion; ~6 s period matches real-time 8.97 m pendulum

stated_facts.said: This Foucault pendulum is 8.97 metres long.

subjects.description: large silver spherical pendulum bob with black top swinging above tiled floor

observation.what_happens: A large silver pendulum bob swings back and forth along a straight line over the tiled floor, moving away from and toward the camera. The free swinging continues throughout the clip, passing over a yellow cross mark while marker pens sit beside the line.

calibration.note: no scale: lengths are in pixels

given: pendulum length = 8.97 m (“This Foucault pendulum is 8.97 metres long.”)
reasoning: The s-channel oscillates with ~6 s period matching sqrt(L/g) for L=8.97 m, centred near -180 pixels not 0, with almost no decay over 29 s. We use s-pixel oscillator dynamics centred at s_eq to avoid an unknown pixel-to-metre scale, starting from ideal harmonic then adding linear viscous and quadratic air drag allowed on Earth in air.

law.title: Harmonic pendulum in metres with general pinhole projection
law.summary: The bob swings harmonically in metres toward and away from the camera, and a pinhole camera turns that into a pixel position that varies as one over its distance, growing near the camera and shrinking far away.

critique.finding: The big bob swings like an ideal tiny swing pulled by gravity of {g} on a line of {L} seen through a pinhole camera shaped by {s0} and {A} and {b}. It only partly captures the motion, leaving regular wavy misses.
critique.headline: Silver pendulum swings on, but simple view falls short
critique.revision_idea: Replace the small-angle spring with the exact sine pull of a real pendulum. The misses wave back and forth at the swing pace, which is exactly what a sine curve leaves behind when you fit it with a straight line.
critique.why_it_won: It lets distant motion look smaller through the camera while the plain pendulums assume what you see is what you get.

preRevision.revision_idea: Add pinhole perspective so pixel position scales with inverse distance for motion toward the camera. The misses repeat every swing and peak at the far and near turning points, which is exactly what a linear-in-pixels law leaves when the true swing is harmonic in meters.

postRevision.revision_idea: Replace the small-angle spring with the exact sine pull of a real pendulum. The misses wave back and forth at the swing pace, which is exactly what a sine curve leaves behind when you fit it with a straight line.

headline: Silver pendulum swings on, but simple view falls short
finding: The big bob swings like an ideal tiny swing pulled by gravity of 9.683 ± 0.019 m/s² on a line of 8.97 m seen through a pinhole camera shaped by 1120 ± 230 px and -1260 ± 220 px and 0 ± 290 1/px. It only partly captures the motion, leaving regular wavy misses.

eyeball.confidence: medium-low: about 7 swings in 300 frames at 7.1 fps gives T~6.0s; image amplitude a few hundred px
eyeball.law_in_words: Small-angle simple pendulum period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), with L=8.97 m, T measured frame-by-frame from far-to-far turning points, so g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2; s_eq is image-plane position of vertical plumb along track relative to first-frame bob position.

wonder.idea: Add pinhole perspective so pixel position scales with inverse distance for motion toward the camera. The misses repeat every swing and peak at the far and near turning points, which is exactly what a linear-in-pixels law leaves when the true swing is harmonic in meters.

truth.note: Real footage of a museum pendulum. The length (8.97 m) and period (6.0 s) are the figures the filmmaker published with the video on Wikimedia Commons; Ansatz was told the length and nothing else. Earth's gravity there is 9.81 m/s² to the precision shown.
